chapter_title: Your First C++ Class in Unreal Engine 5

screens.title: Your First C++ Class in Unreal Engine 5
screens.subtitle: From Editor wizard to an editable, Blueprint-ready Actor

narration.text: In this chapter you'll build a working C++ Actor that the Unreal Editor and Blueprints can use. We start from the New C++ Class wizard, select Actor as the base, and explore how the reflection macros make C++ classes visible and editable. You'll learn why designers often prefer Blueprints for rapid iteration, and why performance-sensitive or core systems belong in C++. We'll add properties with the UPROPERTY macro so values appear in the Details Panel, and functions with UFUNCTION so Blueprints or the editor can call them. You'll also implement BeginPlay and Tick to control runtime behavior and use simple debug printing so you can verify behavior in the editor. Along the way we'll examine common mistakes like forgetting the generated header include or omitting UPROPERTY, and practice a hands-on example that prints a property value. By the end, you will be comfortable creating AActor-derived classes, exposing editable fields, and wiring simple methods for editor and Blueprint use. Try to think in terms of what belongs in C++ versus Blueprints as you follow the steps — which parts need fast iteration, and which need C++ control?

keyIdea.title: What you'll master
keyIdea.text: Create an AActor-derived C++ class, expose properties and functions to the Editor and Blueprints, and implement basic lifecycle methods so your actor interacts at runtime.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: Over the next lesson you'll move from theory to practice. First, you'll differentiate when to use C++ versus Blueprints, understanding each tool's strengths. Second, you'll create a new C++ class derived from AActor inside the Unreal Editor and inspect the generated header and source files. Third, you'll use the UCLASS, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION macros correctly so your class and members are visible to the editor and Blueprints. Finally, you'll implement common lifecycle methods like BeginPlay and Tick, and verify behavior using on-screen debug messages and logs. Each objective focuses on practical skill: creating files, applying macros with correct specifiers, and confirming runtime behavior. These skills matter because they let you balance performance and iteration: put heavy or foundational code in C++, and expose safe hooks to designers through Blueprints. As you work, check for common mistakes like missing the generated header include or skipping UPROPERTY — these prevent the Editor from recognizing your members. By the end you'll have a test actor in a level that demonstrates each capability and a mental checklist for when to prefer C++ or Blueprint.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Steps
screens.subtitle: A hands-on checklist to guide your coding session

narration.text: This second objectives slide gives a concrete checklist you can follow in the editor. First, open the New C++ Class wizard and choose Actor as the base. This creates a header and source file named for your class. Second, add UCLASS with Blueprintable and BlueprintType if you want Blueprints to inherit or use your type. Third, declare UPROPERTY variables with EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite to allow designers to edit per-instance values and Blueprints to read and write them; place them in a Category to keep the Details Panel organized. Fourth, add UFUNCTION with BlueprintCallable for functions you want designers or Blueprints to invoke. As you work, compile from the editor and drag the actor into your level to test. If the property isn’t visible, check that UPROPERTY is present and that the generated header include exists at the end of your header file. This checklist maps directly to the hands-on activity you will complete, and following it reduces common syntax and reflection mistakes while reinforcing why each macro matters in practice.

screens.title: C++ Classes versus Blueprints
screens.subtitle: When to choose C++ and when to use Blueprints in a project

narration.text: C++ and Blueprints are complementary tools. C++ excels at performance-critical systems, complex algorithms, and engine-level modifications where precise control over memory, execution, or low-level APIs is needed. Blueprints excel at rapid prototyping, designer-driven iteration, and creating gameplay that artists and level designers can tweak without recompiling. A hybrid approach is common: place core systems and heavy computations in C++, and expose configurable properties and event hooks to Blueprints so designers can iterate safely. A concrete example from this chapter is implementing an interactive actor: the calculation of an interaction check might live in C++ for speed, while a visual response or designer-tunable range is exposed via UPROPERTY and adjusted in Blueprints. A common misconception is thinking Blueprints are only for simple tasks; they are robust, but they cost performance when doing heavy per-frame work. Conversely, another mistake is putting everything in C++ without exposing easy customization points — that slows designer workflows. The rule of thumb is to evaluate whether a piece of logic needs low-level control or fast iteration, then split responsibilities accordingly. As you plan your first actor, ask: which parts must be fast and which should be editable by designers?

keyIdea.title: Use the right tool
keyIdea.text: Keep performance-sensitive code in C++, expose parameters and simple behaviors to Blueprints for iteration and designer control.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › C++ vs Blueprints
C++ (Core Systems)
Precise control, better performance, suitable for complex algorithms and engine changes. Use it for per-frame heavy logic or memory-sensitive code.
Example
Implement interaction distance calculations and optimized search in C++ so they run fast every frame.
Common mistake
Putting designer-editable fields only in C++ with no exposure makes iteration slow for artists.
Blueprints (Iteration)
Fast to prototype, visual, and accessible to non-programmers. Ideal for event wiring, tuning, and designer-controlled behaviors.
Example
Expose an interaction range via UPROPERTY and let designers adjust it in the Details Panel or Blueprint child.
Common misconception
Thinking Blueprints cannot scale — they can, but heavy per-frame logic is better in C++.
Analogy
Treat C++ as the engine room and Blueprints as the control panel. Place heavy machinery in the engine room and let designers flip switches on the panel.

screens.title: Create a New C++ Class in the Editor
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: New C++ Class wizard to generated files

narration.text: Creating a new C++ class is a guided process in the Unreal Editor. Start by selecting File then New C++ Class, choose Actor as the base for objects you can place into a level, name the class MyFirstActor, and click Create Class. The Editor invokes the Unreal Build Tool and generates two files: a header and a source. The header contains the class declaration and the required UCLASS macro. The source contains method implementations and the constructor. Open both files in your IDE; they will include comments and function stubs for BeginPlay and Tick. A key requirement in headers is placing the generated header include at the end — the file with generated reflection data. If omitted, the editor will not compile reflection metadata and your macros won't work. After modifying files, compile from the Editor so the new type is registered; then open the Content Browser and drag the class into a level to create an instance. This process ensures the Editor knows about your class and that instances can be configured in the Details Panel. Practice this sequence until it becomes second nature: wizard, inspect files, add macros, compile, drop into level, test.

keyIdea.title: Creation sequence
keyIdea.text: Use the New C++ Class wizard, inspect the generated header and source, compile in the Editor, and test the actor in a level.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Create Class
Wizard Steps
  1. 1. File → New C++ Class → choose Actor base.
  2. 2. Name the class MyFirstActor and create it.
  3. 3. Let the Editor generate the header and source files.
  4. 4. Open files in your IDE and inspect stubs like BeginPlay and Tick.
  5. 5. Compile in Editor and drag the actor into your level.
Why this matters
Following the full flow registers your class with the engine and ensures reflection metadata is generated correctly.
Quick checklist
  • Confirm #include "YourClass.generated.h" is present and last.
  • Verify UCLASS macro above the class declaration.
  • Compile and watch the Output Log for reflection errors.
Misstep to avoid
Modifying files before the build finishes can cause missing generated headers until the build is complete.

screens.title: Understanding AActor and Common Base Classes
screens.subtitle: What AActor represents and when to use APawn, ACharacter, and UActorComponent

narration.text: An AActor is any object that can be placed or spawned into a level — props, lights, pickups, or interactive elements. Use AActor for general-purpose objects that need to exist in the world and track state or behavior. If you need player or AI control, APawn is a specialized base for entities that can be possessed by controllers. ACharacter builds on APawn and adds movement components suitable for humanoid characters, including built-in movement replicated across networking. UActorComponent is not an Actor itself; it’s a reusable piece of functionality that attaches to an Actor, like health, inventory, or perception. Choosing the right base class matters because it determines available systems and the lifetime hooks you should expect. For our first class we pick AActor because it’s the simplest container for placeable objects and demonstrates exposing properties. A common misconception is treating Actor components as standalone Actors — components require an owning Actor and their references are managed by UPROPERTY to participate in garbage collection. When you design your interactive actor, think: does the entity need to be possessed, move with Character movement, or simply be placed and interacted with? That decision guides correct base class selection and simplifies later development.

keyIdea.title: Base class choice
keyIdea.text: AActor for placeable objects, APawn for possessable entities, ACharacter for movement-enabled characters, and UActorComponent for attachable reusable behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Base Classes
AActor
Placeable or spawnable objects in a level. Use for props, triggers, and interactive items.
APawn
Entities that can be possessed by a controller. Suitable for player or AI-controlled actors.
ACharacter
Specialized pawn with movement components for walking, jumping, and replicated movement logic.
UActorComponent
Attach reusable behavior to Actors. Components must be referenced with UPROPERTY to ensure proper lifetime management.
Quick decision guide
If the object is placeable and needs minimal control, choose AActor. If it needs to be possessed, choose APawn or ACharacter. If you need reusable behavior, extract a UActorComponent.

screens.title: UCLASS() and Reflection
screens.subtitle: Why the UCLASS macro is required and how specifiers change behavior

narration.text: The UCLASS macro marks a C++ class for Unreal's reflection system. Reflection makes your class recognizable by the Editor, enables serialization, and allows the garbage collector to manage UObject references. Without UCLASS, the Editor will not list your type and macros like UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION will not be processed. You can add specifiers inside the UCLASS parentheses to change how the class is used. For example, Blueprintable allows Blueprints to inherit from your C++ class, and BlueprintType lets variables of the class be used in Blueprints. A practical example is declaring UCLASS(Blueprintable, BlueprintType) for an Actor you expect designers to subclass in Blueprint. A common confusion is thinking UCLASS alone makes member properties visible — you still need UPROPERTY on fields. Also, the generated header include must be the last include in your header file; that file contains code generated by the Unreal Build Tool that wires reflection metadata. Remember: UCLASS enables editor features, specifiers tune usability, and UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION control member exposure. When in doubt, add Blueprintable and BlueprintType for broad editor interoperability during early development. UCLASS() and Reflection means uclass activates unreal's reflection for a c++ class; specifiers like blueprintable and blueprinttype control blueprint interoperability.. In practical terms, why the uclass macro is required and how specifiers change behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reflection anchor
keyIdea.text: UCLASS activates Unreal's reflection for a C++ class; specifiers like Blueprintable and BlueprintType control Blueprint interoperability.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › UCLASS()
What it does
Enables reflection so the Editor can see, serialize, and manage the class. Required for UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION to work.
Example specifiers
Blueprintable, BlueprintType — add them when you want Blueprint subclasses or Blueprint variables that reference the type.
Pitfalls
Forgetting the generated header include or adding macros incorrectly will prevent reflection data from being produced at build time.
Check this
Make sure #include "YourClass.generated.h" is the last include in the header file.
Analogy
Think of UCLASS as registering the class with the engine's directory so the Editor can list and interact with it. Specifiers control what registry notes are added.

screens.title: UPROPERTY: Exposing Variables to the Editor
screens.subtitle: Specifiers, categories, and making values editable and safe

narration.text: UPROPERTY is the macro you use to expose a C++ member variable to Unreal's reflection system. By adding UPROPERTY before a field, you tell the engine how that variable should appear in the Details Panel and how Blueprints can access it. Common specifiers include EditAnywhere so designers can edit the property on any instance, VisibleAnywhere to show but not edit, BlueprintReadOnly to allow Blueprints to read a value, and BlueprintReadWrite to let Blueprints read and modify it. You can also add Category to group properties under a named header in the Details Panel. A concrete example is adding a float MyFloatValue with UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "My Properties") so level designers can adjust it per instance and Blueprints can read and modify it. A common error is forgetting UPROPERTY entirely; the variable will behave like a normal C++ field and won't appear in the editor. Another pitfall is using EditAnywhere for values that should be shared defaults — in that case EditDefaultsOnly may be more appropriate. Use categories to keep the Details Panel readable and to communicate intent to designers.

keyIdea.title: Expose fields safely
keyIdea.text: Use UPROPERTY with appropriate specifiers to control editability, Blueprint access, and organization in the Details Panel.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › UPROPERTY()
Common Specifiers
  • EditAnywhere — editable per instance in the Details Panel.
  • VisibleAnywhere — visible but not editable.
  • BlueprintReadOnly — Blueprints can read the value.
  • BlueprintReadWrite — Blueprints can read and modify the value.
Organization
Use Category="My Custom Category" to group related properties and make the Details Panel clearer for designers.
Example
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "GameFramework/Actor.h"
#include "MyFirstActor.generated.h"

UCLASS(Blueprintable, BlueprintType)
class MYFIRSTCPPPROJECT_API AMyFirstActor : public AActor
{
  GENERATED_BODY()

public:
  AMyFirstActor();

  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "My Properties")
  float MyFloatValue;

  virtual void BeginPlay() override;
  virtual void Tick(float DeltaTime) override;
};
This header shows a float exposed with EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite so it is editable and accessible to Blueprints.

screens.title: UFUNCTION: Make Methods Blueprint-Callable
screens.subtitle: Expose functions safely and understand common specifiers

narration.text: UFUNCTION exposes C++ methods to the reflection system so Blueprints or the editor can call them. Use BlueprintCallable to allow execution from Blueprint graphs, and BlueprintPure for read-only functions that do not modify object state and return a value. Networking specifiers exist as well, such as Server, Client, and NetMulticast, but those are for replication concerns beyond this chapter's hands-on activity. A practical example from our chapter is declaring a function PrintMyMessage with UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "My Functions") so designers can trigger it from a Blueprint or, in some editor contexts, from a function button. When implementing such functions, make sure any UObject references are handled via UPROPERTY if they are stored, so the garbage collector keeps them alive. A common misconception is using BlueprintPure for functions that change state — that will confuse Blueprint flow. Another pitfall is forgetting to mark string parameters correctly or to use const references for heavy types; prefer const FString& when accepting text parameters. The key takeaway is: use UFUNCTION with the right specifier to safely expose behavior and document intent with categories. UFUNCTION: Make Methods Blueprint-Callable means use ufunction specifiers like blueprintcallable and blueprintpure to control how c++ functions appear and behave in blueprints.. In practical terms, expose functions safely and understand common specifiers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Expose behavior
keyIdea.text: Use UFUNCTION specifiers like BlueprintCallable and BlueprintPure to control how C++ functions appear and behave in Blueprints.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › UFUNCTION()
Common Specifiers
  • BlueprintCallable — callable from Blueprints.
  • BlueprintPure — read-only function returning a value, no execution pins in Blueprint.
  • Server/Client/NetMulticast — used for networked functions (advanced).
Parameter tips
Use const references for large types and mark UObject inputs carefully to avoid lifetime issues.
Example Declaration
UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "My Functions")
void PrintMyMessage();
Marking a method this way makes it visible to Blueprint graphs and editor call sites that support function invocation.

screens.title: Implementing MyFirstActor: Constructor, BeginPlay, Tick
screens.subtitle: See how default values and lifecycle hooks are implemented in source

narration.text: After declaring your class, implement the constructor and lifecycle methods in the source file. The constructor typically sets default values and configures tick behavior, for example enabling tick with PrimaryActorTick. bCanEverTick = true and setting a default for MyFloatValue to 100.0. BeginPlay is called when the actor begins play, either at level start or when spawned; it is a reliable place to initialize runtime state and to emit a startup message so you can confirm the actor is active. Using the engine's debug message facility, you can show a short on-screen message and write to the log to confirm behavior. Tick runs every frame while enabled and is appropriate for continuous updates, but be cautious — heavy logic here impacts performance. Finally, implement PrintMyMessage with BlueprintCallable to show the current value of MyFloatValue both on screen and in the log. A common misconception is using Tick for rare updates; prefer event-driven approaches whenever possible. The concrete example in the source prints a green message at begin play and a yellow message when calling PrintMyMessage, helping you verify both automatic and manual activations.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle basics
keyIdea.text: Set defaults in the constructor, initialize runtime state in BeginPlay, and use Tick only for continuous updates. Use debug prints to validate behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Lifecycle
MyFirstActor.cpp (excerpt)
#include "MyFirstActor.h"
#include "Engine/Engine.h"

AMyFirstActor::AMyFirstActor()
{
  PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true;
  MyFloatValue = 100.0f;
}

void AMyFirstActor::BeginPlay()
{
  Super::BeginPlay();
  if (GEngine)
  {
    GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage(-1, 5.f, FColor::Green, TEXT("MyFirstActor has begun play!"));
  }
  UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("MyFirstActor has begun play from C++ log!"));
}

void AMyFirstActor::Tick(float DeltaTime)
{
  Super::Tick(DeltaTime);
  // per-frame logic
}

void AMyFirstActor::PrintMyMessage()
{
  if (GEngine)
  {
    GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage(-1, 5.f, FColor::Yellow, FString::Printf(TEXT("MyFloatValue is: %f"), MyFloatValue));
  }
  UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("PrintMyMessage called. MyFloatValue: %f"), MyFloatValue);
}
Explanation and Tips
  • Constructor sets defaults and tick behavior before BeginPlay runs.
  • BeginPlay is ideal for runtime initialization and one-time debug messages.
  • Use Tick sparingly; prefer events for infrequent updates.
  • Use GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage plus UE_LOG to validate both on-screen and log output.
Check your understanding
Why would you use BeginPlay instead of the constructor for runtime initialization? Think about lifecycle timing and engine state.

screens.title: Build MyInteractiveActor (Header)
screens.subtitle: Add InteractionRange property and Interact function to the header

narration.text: In this hands-on header example you'll add a property InteractionRange and a BlueprintCallable Interact method. Start by marking your class with UCLASS(Blueprintable, BlueprintType) so designers can subtype it. Declare a float InteractionRange with UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Interaction") so level designers can adjust the value per instance and Blueprints can read or set it. Next declare a UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Interaction") void Interact(const FString& PlayerName) to accept a player's name and log or show a message. The header should still include the generated header file as the final include. This design separates data (InteractionRange) from behavior (Interact), making the actor both configurable and callable from Blueprints or editor commands. A common mistake when adding a string parameter is passing by value instead of const reference, which can copy unnecessarily. Prefer const FString& for efficiency. After editing the header, save and switch to the source file to provide implementations, then compile from the editor and test by dragging the actor into the world and calling Interact from an editor button or Blueprint. Build MyInteractiveActor (Header) means declare interactionrange with editanywhere and interact as blueprintcallable to allow designer tuning and runtime calls from blueprints.. In practical terms, add interactionrange property and interact function to the header. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Header changes
keyIdea.text: Declare InteractionRange with EditAnywhere and Interact as BlueprintCallable to allow designer tuning and runtime calls from Blueprints.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Header: Interaction
MyInteractiveActor.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "GameFramework/Actor.h"
#include "MyInteractiveActor.generated.h"

UCLASS(Blueprintable, BlueprintType)
class MYFIRSTCPPPROJECT_API AMyInteractiveActor : public AActor
{
  GENERATED_BODY()

public:
  AMyInteractiveActor();

  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Interaction")
  float InteractionRange;

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Interaction")
  void Interact(const FString& PlayerName);

protected:
  virtual void BeginPlay() override;

public:
  virtual void Tick(float DeltaTime) override;
};
Why const reference
Passing PlayerName as const FString& avoids unnecessary copies and is a recommended convention for input strings in Unreal C++ headers.

screens.title: Build MyInteractiveActor (Source)
screens.subtitle: Implement constructor defaults and Interact behavior, then compile and test

narration.text: With the header complete, implement the constructor and Interact method in the source file. In the constructor set PrimaryActorTick. bCanEverTick to true if you need per-frame behavior, and set InteractionRange to a sensible default such as 200.0. Implement Interact to use the engine's debug messaging to inform you which player triggered it and the current InteractionRange. Use GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage for visible feedback during play and UE_LOG for persistent logs in the Output Log. After saving, compile from the Unreal Editor. If compilation succeeds, drag an instance of MyInteractiveActor into the level. Select it and inspect the Details Panel to confirm InteractionRange appears under Interaction. Use the editor's function call control or a Blueprint to call Interact with a sample name like PlayerOne and observe the on-screen message and the log entry. If the function or property doesn't appear, recheck UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION presence and confirm that the generated header include was not accidentally moved. This loop — edit, compile, place, test — is the core iteration pattern you will use frequently. Build MyInteractiveActor (Source) means set defaults in the constructor, implement interact to print messages, compile in-editor, then place and invoke the actor to validate the features.. In practical terms, implement constructor defaults and interact behavior, then compile and test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Source & Test
keyIdea.text: Set defaults in the constructor, implement Interact to print messages, compile in-editor, then place and invoke the actor to validate the features.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Source: Interaction
MyInteractiveActor.cpp
#include "MyInteractiveActor.h"
#include "Engine/Engine.h"

AMyInteractiveActor::AMyInteractiveActor()
{
  PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true;
  InteractionRange = 200.0f;
}

void AMyInteractiveActor::BeginPlay()
{
  Super::BeginPlay();
}

void AMyInteractiveActor::Tick(float DeltaTime)
{
  Super::Tick(DeltaTime);
}

void AMyInteractiveActor::Interact(const FString& PlayerName)
{
  if (GEngine)
  {
    GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage(-1, 5.f, FColor::Cyan, 
      FString::Printf(TEXT("%s interacted with %s! Range: %.2f"), *PlayerName, *GetName(), InteractionRange));
  }
  UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("%s interacted with %s! Range: %.2f"), *PlayerName, *GetName(), InteractionRange);
}
Testing Checklist
  • Compile from the Unreal Editor until the build completes.
  • Drag MyInteractiveActor into the level and select it.
  • Confirm InteractionRange appears under the Interaction category in Details Panel.
  • Call Interact with a sample player name and observe on-screen feedback and log entries.
If something fails
Check for missing UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION macros, misplaced generated header include, and review compiler output for reflection errors.

screens.title: Troubleshooting and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Errors to watch for and practical tips for smooth iteration

narration.text: When working with Unreal C++ reflection and editor exposure, a few mistakes recur. First, forgetting to include the generated header as the last include in your header file prevents reflection metadata, so UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION won't be processed. Second, omitting UPROPERTY on fields you expect to see in the Details Panel means they'll remain ordinary C++ variables. Third, using Tick for heavy logic leads to performance issues; avoid per-frame work unless necessary. Fourth, using the wrong specifier, for example BlueprintReadOnly when you need BlueprintReadWrite, will cause confusion and extra edits. To avoid these, follow these best practices: always verify generated includes, use categories to organize properties, choose EditAnywhere for per-instance editability, and prefer events or timers over Tick for infrequent updates. When compilation fails, read the build log for reflection errors — they often point to misplaced macros or invalid specifier syntax. Finally, test iteratively: compile, place an actor, inspect the Details Panel, and invoke functions. This rapid loop surfaces mistakes quickly and helps you learn how macros affect editor behavior. Troubleshooting and Best Practices means always verify generated header placement, presence of uproperty/ufunction, correct specifiers, and avoid heavy tick usage for performance.. In practical terms, errors to watch for and practical tips for smooth iteration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Keep a checklist
keyIdea.text: Always verify generated header placement, presence of UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION, correct specifiers, and avoid heavy Tick usage for performance.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Troubleshooting
Common Errors
  • Missing generated header include stops reflection code generation.
  • Forgotten UPROPERTY means the field won't appear in the Editor.
  • Incorrect specifier syntax causes build-time reflection errors.
  • Heavy Tick logic degrades performance if run every frame unnecessarily.
Best Practices
  • Keep generated include last in the header.
  • Group properties using Category to help designers.
  • Use BlueprintCallable for functions designers should trigger.
  • Prefer events, timers, or delegates over Tick when possible.
Quick recovery
If reflection errors occur, check the header for misplaced macros or invalid specifier lists, fix the issue, recompile, and recheck the editor for the property/function presence.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three core takeaways from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the three essential ideas from this chapter. First, the UCLASS macro is required to register your C++ class with Unreal's reflection system so the Editor and Blueprints can recognize it. Second, UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION allow you to expose variables and methods with specifiers like EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, and BlueprintCallable to control editability and accessibility. Third, lifecycle hooks — the constructor, BeginPlay, and Tick — let you set defaults, initialize runtime state, and run per-frame logic; use Tick sparingly and prefer event-driven updates when possible. Each of these items is a practical tool: use UCLASS to make the class visible, UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION to make its members useful to designers, and lifecycle methods to orchestrate behavior. Keep these points handy while you create MyFirstActor or MyInteractiveActor and test iteratively in the Editor. Which of these will you practice first: exposing a property or creating a BlueprintCallable function?

keyIdea.title: Three essentials
keyIdea.text: Reflection with UCLASS, exposure with UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION, and lifecycle control with constructor/BeginPlay/Tick.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Key Concepts
UCLASS()
Registers a C++ class with Unreal's reflection system so the Editor can use it.
UPROPERTY() / UFUNCTION()
Expose variables and methods to the Editor and Blueprints with controlled access.
Lifecycle
Constructor sets defaults; BeginPlay initializes runtime state; Tick updates per frame when enabled.
Summary

Combine C++ control with Blueprint exposure: write core logic in C++ and expose simple, safe hooks for designers to tune and extend.

narration.text: As you proceed, keep three condensed reminders in mind. First, always place the generated header include at the end of your header file to ensure reflection metadata is created. Second, use UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION with the correct specifiers to control what designers can edit and call — EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite are common choices for editable properties. Third, test iteratively by compiling in the Editor, placing your Actor in a level, and using on-screen debug messages plus logs to confirm behavior. These short habits prevent common blockers and make C++ and Blueprints work together smoothly. Before you finish a change, ask: will this need designer tuning? If yes, expose it with UPROPERTY. Will it be invoked by a designer or Blueprint? If yes, add UFUNCTION. This small checklist accelerates reliable development and collaboration across programmers and designers.

keyIdea.title: Developer checklist
keyIdea.text: Generated header last, use proper UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION specifiers, and iterate by compiling and testing in the Editor.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Quick Reminders
Generated Header
Always include the generated header as the last include in your .h file.
Expose Right
Use EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite for designer-tunable variables; use BlueprintCallable for functions designers should trigger.
Iterate Fast
Compile from the Editor, place the actor, inspect Details Panel, and invoke functions to validate behavior quickly.
Final Tip

Small, consistent practices save time: reflection setup, correct specifiers, and iterative testing are your core workflow for reliable C++ + Blueprint integration.
